name: CUBA

flag.title: The Cuban Flag
flag.note: Blue & white stripes, red triangle, star

lead: Cuba is the Caribbean's biggest island, where candy-coloured vintage cars rumble past crumbling-beautiful buildings and music leaks from every doorway. Havana, its capital, overflows with dancers and sea-salt air. The island grows sugar cane, makes world-famous cigars, and hides mountains, caves, and coral reefs waiting to be explored.
geo: Cuba is a long, thin island — 1,200 km from end to end but rarely more than 100 km wide. The Escambray and Sierra Maestra mountains rise in the south-east, draped in cloud forest, while the north coast opens onto calm turquoise sea.
Inland, broad plains were once carpeted in sugar cane. Cuba claims more than 4,000 smaller islets, plus spectacular limestone caves, underground rivers, and coral reefs teeming with fish.
animals: Cuba's star creature is the bee hummingbird — the world's tiniest bird, barely bigger than a bumblebee, weighing less than a paperclip. The Cuban solenodon is a shrew-like mammal so ancient it scarcely changed since dinosaur times.

Flamingos wade in rosy flocks along the northern cays. Cuban crocodiles — stocky and bright-eyed — splash through freshwater swamps and are found nowhere else on Earth. Manatees, hawksbill turtles, and whale sharks patrol the surrounding sea.
culture: Cubans are passionate about music — son, salsa, and rumba were all born here. Any street corner can turn into a dance floor. Baseball is the national sport; kids practise from the moment they can hold a bat.
Food is hearty: black beans and rice (moros y cristianos), fried plantain, and slow-roasted pork. Cigars hand-rolled in the Vuelta Abajo region are considered the finest on the planet.
history: Cuba was home to the Taíno people before Columbus landed in 1492. Spain ruled for nearly 400 years, building wealth on sugar plantations worked by enslaved Africans — a legacy that shaped Cuban culture, food, and music.

After a fierce independence struggle, Cuba broke free from Spain in 1898. In 1959, Fidel Castro's revolution turned the island into a communist state. That system still governs today, making Cuba one of the world's most singular countries.
wows: The bee hummingbird, only found in Cuba, is the world's smallest bird — lighter than a coin.
Cuba sends more doctors abroad to help other nations than almost any country on Earth.
Havana's 1950s American cars still run daily because imports were banned for decades.
Cuba was once the world's top sugar exporter, covering huge swaths of land in cane.
The Monte Iberia eleuth frog, found in Cuba, is one of the world's tiniest vertebrates.
A 1961 literacy campaign sent students island-wide, lifting the rate from 23% to 96%.
Cuba sits in a hurricane hotspot, yet its evacuation system is globally praised for saving lives.

myths.myth: All Cubans smoke cigars every day
myths.fact: Cigars are a famous export, but most Cubans rarely smoke them — they're expensive and made largely for overseas buyers.
Vintage cars are real, but Cuba also has modern hospitals, universities, biotech labs, and growing internet access.
